title: Is a Noisy Classroom a Thinking Classroom?
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick challenges the long-standing classroom-observation assumption that noise is a visible proxy for thinking, using a new study (Marko et al., 2026, in Cognition) which found that when students try to retrieve concepts from memory to generate new ideas, the greatest interference comes not from meaningless environmental sound but from meaningful background speech. The brain processes speech for meaning automatically and involuntarily, creating competing activity in the same semantic-processing systems needed for effortful thinking -- and the effect grows worse as thinking becomes more effortful and as background speech becomes more topically related to the task at hand. Hendrick connects this to Peter Liljedahl's Building Thinking Classrooms model, arguing that the visible, audible signs of engagement (animated group discussion) can actually work against the invisible cognitive work of working memory and semantic retrieval that constitutes real academic reasoning. He is careful to stop short of dismissing classroom talk altogether, calling instead for "cognitive hospitality" -- environments that deliberately move between collaborative and quiet modes depending on the cognitive demand of the task.
points: The study's central finding inverts a common classroom-observation heuristic: meaningful background speech interferes with effortful thinking far more than meaningless ambient noise, because the brain processes speech automatically regardless of intent to attend to it.

Interference gets worse, not better, when background talk is topically related to the task at hand -- meaning "productive classroom chatter" on a similar topic is exactly the condition that maximally disrupts a neighbouring student's thinking.

Hendrick applies the finding directly to Peter Liljedahl's Building Thinking Classrooms, arguing its visible markers of engagement (standing, talking, clustering) may work against the very working-memory processes needed for academic reasoning.

His proposed resolution, "cognitive hospitality," avoids an anti-talk overcorrection -- the goal is classrooms that move fluidly between collaborative and quiet modes depending on whether ideas need sharing or concepts need consolidating.
quotes: When I first started teaching English 20 years ago, a fairly uncontested idea was the notion that “a noisy classroom is a thinking classroom”.
A new study in Cognition (Marko et al., 2026) shows just how costly that particular noise can be if students are trying to think hard about something.

The researchers found that when we are trying to retrieve certain concepts from memory to generate new ideas, the greatest interference comes not from meaningless sounds (traffic, humming, background tones etc), but surprisingly from meaningful speech.
This creates interference not by stealing attention, but by creating competing neural activity in the same systems you need for thinking.
Students discussing related topics create maximum interference for peers working on similar material - exactly the opposite of what we’d assume about “productive classroom talk.
Rather, it’s a call for cognitive hospitality; creating learning environments that honour both the social and solitary dimensions of thinking.
